title: Building a Framework-Based Application
learning_outcomes: Explain what building a framework-based application contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: routing and controllers.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Frameworks provide conventions and reusable components for routing, dependency management, validation, persistence, and queues. Learn the underlying HTTP/security concepts first and verify the selected framework's supported versions. In this lesson, focus on routing and controllers; then compare it with authentication and authorization. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use building a framework-based application when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Frameworks provide conventions and reusable components for routing, dependency management, validation, persistence, and queues. Learn the underlying HTTP/security concepts first and verify the selected framework's supported versions. For building a framework-based application, begin with routing and controllers. Also distinguish authentication and authorization; database integration; validation and error handling. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: Routing and controllers
items.text: Track where this value enters the request lifecycle and where it affects the response; client-provided data must be treated as untrusted.

items.title: Authentication and authorization
items.text: Distinguish identity verification from resource permission, and test expiry, invalid credentials, and denied access as well as the success path.

items.title: Database integration
items.text: Keep query structure separate from data values, check failures explicitly, and use constraints or transactions when integrity depends on multiple operations.

items.title: Validation and error handling
items.text: Know when to use validation and error handling, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Testing, deployment, and maintainability
items.text: Write an assertion about observable behavior and include a boundary or failure case; a passing command alone does not prove the requirement.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Building a Framework-Based Application

$steps = ["begin transaction", "validate changes", "commit or roll back"];
echo implode(" -> ", $steps) . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for building a framework-based application from top to bottom. Start by identifying routing and controllers, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

At least one edge case is tested or documented.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
